whatTheyArgued: Berge's Graphes et hypergraphes (Dunod 1970; English 1973) generalizes graphs so an edge (hyperedge) may join any number of vertices, not just two; the arXiv review I searched (not readable as text) and catalog records confirm the book and its dates. I did not read Berge. The manifest is copyrighted_deferred. Whether he first coined 'hypergraph' in 1970 is a gap: other sources date his work to 1967 and 1973 and a Berge-led Hypergraph Seminar in 1972 (edited 1974), so the 1970 coinage in the compendium is unverified.

scholarship.ref: Hypergraphs: an introduction and review (arXiv 2002.05014), via search digest; PDF unreadable by fetch
scholarship.supports: Berge 1967/1973 introduces hypergraphs to generalize graphs; multi-adic relations
scholarship.disputes: a date inconsistency (1967 vs 1970 vs 1973) across citations; I could not resolve it

ourUse: hypergraph.js: EOHyperedge participants and refs are walked as a hypergraph of observations, mentions, expectations and obligations; edges are n-ary.

bends.ours: Compendium role is 'he coined it'; credit says he coined the hypergraph.
bends.theirs: I verified only that Berge wrote the founding book; priority of the term over Berge's earlier 1967 usage and others was not verified.

bends.ours: Hyperedges as typed participant lists with witness and encounter refs, built for reading.
bends.theirs: Berge's hypergraphs are set systems on a vertex set, with a theory (transversals, colorings, duality); we use none of the theory, only n-ary edges.
